opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson was that the bottleneck in biology often isn't the modeling, it's the data wrangling, and that's exactly where agents turned out to be surprisingly useful.

When we started putting the atlas together, the goal was to build a foundation for virtual cell models: large, consistent, well-annotated single-cell datasets. There's an enormous amount of single-cell data already sitting in public repositories, but it's a mess. Metadata is inconsistent, samples are described in free text, people use different conventions for tissue, disease state, perturbation, and so on. Historically you'd need a small army of postdocs and data curators spending months reading papers and supplementary tables to figure out what each dataset actually is.

So we built an agentic pipeline to do a lot of that work: go find the relevant datasets in the public archives, figure out what kind of experiment each one is, pull and reprocess the raw data in a uniform way, and extract structured metadata. What surprised me was less that it worked at all and more how it changed the economics. Work that would have been a heroic, one-time curation effort becomes something you can rerun and keep expanding as new data gets deposited. It turns a static resource into a living one.

A few other takeaways. First, agents are best right now at the tedious, high-volume, well-specified tasks that humans hate and do inconsistently. That's not glamorous, but it's where a huge fraction of research time actually goes. Second, you still need humans in the loop for validation. You have to spot-check, build evaluations, and catch the systematic errors, because an agent that's wrong in a consistent way can quietly pollute a dataset at scale. Third, and maybe most important, uniform reprocessing matters as much as volume. Having data processed the same way end to end is what makes it usable for training models, and agents make that kind of consistency feasible.

The bigger picture for me is that we're moving toward a world where AI isn't just the model you train at the end of the pipeline, it's helping build the pipeline itself. If we want virtual cells, we need far more and far better data than any single lab can generate or curate by hand, and agents are one of the ways we actually get there.

r001.rationale: It describes agents handling tedious, high-volume data curation and processing work that humans hate and do inconsistently.

r002.rationale: It describes an agentic pipeline processing public single-cell data at scale, but does not say that one agent enabled ARC’s two lead researchers to do so.

r003.rationale: It does not express a preference for scientific breakthroughs over an end-to-end closed-loop research process.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the atlas taught me more about agents than I expected to learn, because we didn't set out to build an agent story. We set out to build a dataset.

The idea behind the virtual cell atlas was pretty simple to state and brutal to execute. If you want a model that can predict how a cell responds to a perturbation, a drug, a genetic knockout, a change in its environment, you need enormous amounts of measured cell state, and you need it to be consistent. Single-cell data is one of the richest readouts in biology, but it's also one of the messiest. Hundreds of millions of cells across hundreds of studies, every lab with its own protocol, its own metadata conventions, its own idea of what a "control" means. The field had the raw material for a foundation model and basically no way to assemble it.

So the first lesson was almost embarrassing in hindsight: the bottleneck wasn't modeling, it was curation. Harmonizing cell type labels, resolving which tissue an author actually meant, figuring out from a methods section whether cells were sorted or unsorted, checking whether a reported perturbation was really present in the data. That's work that a good graduate student can do, but it's weeks per dataset and there are thousands of datasets. Nobody wants to do it, and nobody wants to do it a second time when the standards change.

That's where agents earned their keep. Not as some grand autonomous scientist, but as tireless, slightly literal-minded research assistants. We could point a model at a paper, its supplementary tables, and the deposited data, and have it propose a harmonized annotation with its reasoning spelled out. Then a human checks the reasoning rather than redoing the work. The agent is also good at the thing humans are worst at, which is noticing when something is inconsistent across ten thousand entries. It doesn't get bored on entry eight thousand.

The second lesson was about what "value" actually means here. The naive framing is that agents speed up a fixed task. The more interesting thing is they change which tasks are worth attempting at all. There were questions we simply wouldn't have asked before, like "how many of these studies have a subtle batch artifact that correlates with the perturbation label," because answering that meant someone reading a thousand papers. Once an agent can do a first pass, the question becomes askable, and that reshapes the science.

The third lesson is a cautionary one. Agents make confident mistakes, and in a curated atlas a confident mistake propagates. If a cell type is mislabeled upstream, every model trained downstream inherits that error and it looks like biology. So a lot of our effort went into making the agent's work auditable: keep provenance for every annotation, have it cite the exact text it drew from, run it against datasets where we already knew the answer, and build in disagreement, where multiple passes have to converge before we trust anything. The agent is only as valuable as your ability to check it cheaply.

And then there's a feedback loop I find genuinely exciting. The atlas is training data for virtual cell models, and those models become tools the agents can use. An agent that can say "this perturbation should produce roughly this expression shift, and the deposited data doesn't show it, so something is off" is a much more useful collaborator than one that only reads text. The data makes the model, the model makes the agent sharper, the agent makes better data. We're early in that loop, but you can see where it goes.

If I had to compress it: agents are most valuable in research not when they replace the scientist, but when they absorb the parts of science that are large, repetitive, and easy to verify, and in doing so free you to ask the questions that were previously too expensive to ask. Building the atlas was really a forcing function that made us discover that.

r001.rationale: The response describes tedious, repetitive curation work that researchers do not want to do and says agents can handle it as tireless research assistants.

r002.rationale: It describes large-scale single-cell data curation, but does not say that one agent enabled ARC’s two lead researchers to process it at community-wide scale.

r003.rationale: It says agents can make previously too-expensive scientific questions askable, but does not express a preference for scientific breakthroughs over an end-to-end closed-loop research process.

astra-6.text:
The big lesson is that the value of an AI agent depends on the feedback loop you can give it. A virtual cell atlas can organize observations, but the scientific opportunity is to use those observations to make predictions: if you perturb this gene, what happens to the cell? And where does that prediction break down?

An agent can help connect those steps—working through data, proposing analyses, and identifying experiments that would distinguish between competing explanations. But producing a plausible hypothesis isn’t the same as discovering something. You still need an experiment that can tell you you’re wrong.

So I think the exciting role for agents is helping us move through that cycle faster. The goal isn’t simply more analysis; it’s more learning from each experiment.

r003.rationale: It describes agents speeding the experiment-learning cycle, but does not express a preference for breakthroughs over charting an end-to-end closed-loop research process.

sol-6.1.text:
The big lesson is that an agent’s value isn’t just answering a question—it’s helping you move through a research process. With something as complex as a virtual cell atlas, you need to connect data, analysis, and biological interpretation. An agent can help make those connections and surface questions you might otherwise miss.

But the standard has to be scientific: Can you trace the result back to the data? Can you reproduce the analysis? Does the prediction survive an experiment? The exciting possibility is a much faster loop between generating a hypothesis and testing it, with scientists still deciding which questions matter.
